name: EU AI Act Risk Tiers
question: Does the EU AI Act apply to us, and at what tier?
summary: The EU AI Act classifies AI systems by risk. A few practices are prohibited; high-risk systems, including creditworthiness scoring of individuals and life and health insurance pricing, need risk management, data governance, logging, human oversight and conformity assessment; chatbots and generated content carry transparency duties; everything else is minimal risk. It reaches Indian firms whose systems are used in the EU or whose outputs are used there. The 2026 Digital Omnibus moved Annex III high-risk duties to 2 December 2027.
useCases: Serving EU residents or EU clients
Global banks and brokers with EU operations

items.detail: since 2 Feb 2025; fines up to €35m or 7% of turnover
from 2 Dec 2027; fines up to €15m or 3%
from 2 Aug 2026: say it is AI, label synthetic content
no new duties beyond AI literacy
builds or places it on the market: most duties
uses it: oversight, logs, informing people

steps.title: Scope first
steps.text: The Act reaches providers and deployers outside the EU when the system’s output is used in the EU. The fintech’s scoring of students in Germany is in scope; its Indian-only book is not.

steps.title: A few practices are banned
steps.text: Manipulation, exploiting vulnerabilities, social scoring and emotion recognition at work have been prohibited since 2 February 2025.

steps.title: High-risk: Annex III
steps.text: Creditworthiness scoring of individuals and life and health insurance pricing are high-risk. Fraud detection is carved out of the credit category.

steps.title: Your role sets your duties
steps.text: A provider builds the system and carries the heaviest duties; a deployer uses it and must keep logs, oversee it and inform people.

steps.title: Dates after the Omnibus
steps.text: Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, in force 27 July 2026, moved Annex III high-risk duties to 2 December 2027. Plan backwards from that date.

steps.title: Chatbots: say it is AI
steps.text: Transparency duties apply from 2 August 2026: people must know they are dealing with AI, and synthetic content must be labelled.

practice.scenario: An Indian fintech, fictional, offered a credit line to Indian students studying in Germany through a German partner. Its creditworthiness model now scored EU residents, which makes it a high-risk system under Annex III with the fintech as provider. Its support chatbot needed an AI disclosure from 2 August 2026, and its fraud model was carved out of the credit-scoring category. The team planned documentation, logging and human oversight back from 2 December 2027.

numericDrill.question: A high-risk provider breaches its obligations. The maximum fine is €15 million or 3% of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher. With a turnover of €800 million, what is the maximum fine, in € million?
numericDrill.answer: 3% of €800 million is €24 million, which is higher than €15 million, so the maximum is €24 million. For prohibited practices the ceiling rises to €35 million or 7%, which would be €56 million here.

interview.question: Does the EU AI Act apply to an Indian company?
interview.answer: It can. It applies to providers placing AI systems on the EU market and to providers and deployers outside the EU when the system’s output is used in the EU. An Indian fintech scoring the creditworthiness of EU residents, or a broker serving EU clients through a chatbot, is in scope for those systems.

interview.question: What changed with the Digital Omnibus?
interview.answer: Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, in force from 27 July 2026, moved the high-risk obligations for Annex III systems such as credit scoring to 2 December 2027 and for product-embedded systems to 2 August 2028. Prohibitions have applied since February 2025, and chatbot transparency duties still apply from 2 August 2026.
